knowledge_statements.statement_title: Canonical Newton problem representations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R^q\) be continuously differentiable, let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable, and let \(c:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be twice continuously differentiable. Write \(J_F\) for the Jacobian, \(A=J_c\), and \(\mathcal L(x,\lambda)=f(x)-\lambda^Tc(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, smooth, exact Newton representations for square equations, unconstrained stationarity, and equality-constrained KKT systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A Newton problem representation at a current point is one of the following locally linearized systems. For \(F(x)=0\), the equation representation is \[J_F(x)p=-F(x).\] For unconstrained minimization, applying Newton's method to \(
abla f(x)=0\) gives \[
abla^2f(x)p=-
abla f(x),\] equivalently the stationarity equation of the quadratic model \(m_x(p)=f(x)+
abla f(x)^Tp+	frac12p^T
abla^2f(x)p\). For equality-constrained minimization, applying Newton's method to \(R(x,\lambda)=(
abla_x\mathcal L(x,\lambda),c(x))=0\) gives \[ egin{bmatrix}
abla_{xx}^2\mathcal L(x,\lambda)&-A(x)^T\A(x)&0\end{bmatrix} egin{bmatrix}p\p_\lambda\end{bmatrix}=- egin{bmatrix}
abla_x\mathcal L(x,\lambda)\c(x)\end{bmatrix}.\] These are representations of the same construction: set a first-order affine model of the relevant residual equal to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Newton problem representation is obtained by selecting the residual that characterizes the target problem and setting its affine model to zero. For a square nonlinear equation the residual is the equation map and the Newton system uses its Jacobian. For unconstrained optimization the residual is the gradient, so its Jacobian is the Hessian; the resulting system is also the stationarity equation of the second-order Taylor model. For equality-constrained optimization the residual consists of Lagrangian stationarity together with feasibility, and its Jacobian is the primal-dual KKT matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[J_R(w)\,\Delta w=-R(w)\] is the common residual-linearization form, with the displayed equation, optimization, and KKT systems obtained by the corresponding choices of \(R\) and \(w\).
equivalent_formulations_latex:
For unconstrained optimization, \(
abla^2 f(x)p=-
abla f(x)\) is equivalent to \(
abla_pm_x(p)=0\).
For equality constraints, the Newton-KKT equations are the first-order conditions of the quadratic model of the Lagrangian subject to \(A(x)p+c(x)=0\).
special_cases_latex: Taking \(F=\nabla f\) converts the nonlinear-equation representation into the unconstrained optimization representation.
Taking \(R(x,\lambda)=(\nabla_x\mathcal L(x,\lambda),c(x))\) yields a square primal-dual residual in \(\mathbb R^{n+m}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Whenever the selected residual Jacobian is nonsingular, the exact Newton correction is uniquely defined.
Different algebraic solution methods may be applied without changing the represented Newton correction.
boundary_notes: Rectangular residuals require least-squares, minimum-norm, projection, or generalized-inverse conventions not fixed by this definition.
Inequality constraints introduce sign and complementarity conditions and therefore require an enlarged representation.

notation.meaning: The residual map whose zero characterizes the selected problem.
The multiplier correction in the equality-constrained representation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Newton updates from scalar, system, and stationarity linearizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unified representation of Newton's method by local linearization, together with the unconstrained-optimization specialization obtained from the stationarity equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a scalar equation $\phi(t)=0$, when $\phi'(t_k)\ne0$, Newton's update is
\[
t_{k+1}=t_k-\frac{\phi(t_k)}{\phi'(t_k)}.
\]
For a nonlinear system $F(x)=0$, when $F'(x_k)$ is nonsingular, the corresponding update is
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k-[F'(x_k)]^{-1}F(x_k).
\]
Applying this construction to the unconstrained stationarity equation $\nabla f(x)=0$, when $\nabla^2f(x_k)$ is nonsingular, gives
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k-[\nabla^2f(x_k)]^{-1}\nabla f(x_k).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Newton's method linearizes a scalar equation or nonlinear system and solves the resulting linear equation. Applying system Newton to the stationarity equation for unconstrained minimization produces the classical Hessian-based Newton update.
assumptions_latex: F'(x_k)\text{ is nonsingular for the system update}
\nabla^2f(x_k)\text{ is nonsingular for the unconstrained-minimization update}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: t_{k+1}=t_k-\frac{\phi(t_k)}{\phi'(t_k)},\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k-[F'(x_k)]^{-1}F(x_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k-[\nabla^2f(x_k)]^{-1}\nabla f(x_k)

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Newton system for a nonlinear equation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and let \(F:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuously differentiable. Its Jacobian at \(x\) is \(J_F(x)\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional square nonlinear equations with an exact first derivative; no nonsingularity or convergence assertion is included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(x\in\mathcal D\), the affine residual model is \[M_x(p)=F(x)+J_F(x)p,\qquad x+p\in\mathcal D.\] A Newton correction at \(x\) is any \(p\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \[M_x(p)=0,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad J_F(x)p=-F(x).\] The associated full Newton update is \(x^+=x+p\). Thus the Newton system is the linear system produced by requiring the first-order model of the nonlinear residual to vanish. Existence and uniqueness of the correction are separate properties of \(J_F(x)\), not part of the defining equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuously differentiable square map, the Newton system at a point is obtained by replacing the nonlinear residual at a prospective new point with its affine model and setting that model equal to zero. A Newton correction is any solution of the Jacobian equation, and a full Newton update adds that correction to the current point. The definition permits a singular or inconsistent Jacobian system; whether a correction exists or is unique is determined separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[p\in\{v\in\mathbb R^n:J_F(x)v=-F(x)\},\qquad x^+=x+p.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(J_F(x)p=-F(x)\) is equivalent to \(M_x(p)=0\) for \(M_x(p)=F(x)+J_F(x)p\).
When \(J_F(x)\) is nonsingular, the correction has the explicit form \(p=-J_F(x)^{-1}F(x)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(n=1\), the system is \(F'(x)p=-F(x)\), giving \(x^+=x-F(x)/F'(x)\) when \(F'(x)\ne0\).
For \(F=\nabla f\), the system becomes the unconstrained optimization Newton equation.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(F(x)=0\), then \(p=0\) is a Newton correction.
If \(J_F(x)\) is invertible, exactly one Newton correction exists.
boundary_notes: The definition is for a square map; nonsquare maps need an additional least-squares or minimum-norm convention.
Damping and line searches replace the full update by \(x^+=x+\alpha p\) and are not part of this representation.

notation.meaning: Affine model of the nonlinear residual at the current point.
Jacobian matrix of the residual map.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral Taylor representation and exact Newton step
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral first-order expansion, affine residual model, and the model-root definition of the pure Newton step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$ be continuously differentiable on a convex open set $D$. For $x,x+p\in D$, $$r(x+p)=r(x)+\int_0^1J(x+tp)p\,dt.$$ At an iterate $x_k\in D$, the affine Newton model is $$M_k(p)=r(x_k)+J(x_k)p.$$ Pure Newton chooses $p_k$ so that $M_k(p_k)=0$; if $J(x_k)$ is nonsingular, this uniquely gives $$p_k=-J(x_k)^{-1}r(x_k),$$ equivalently $J(x_k)p_k=-r(x_k)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuously differentiable residual map on a convex open set has an integral first-order expansion along each segment in the set. Freezing its Jacobian at the current iterate gives the affine Newton model. Pure Newton sets that model to zero, and a nonsingular Jacobian yields the unique inverse-form step.
assumptions_latex: r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is continuously differentiable on a convex open set }D
J(x_k)\text{ is nonsingular for the unique inverse-form step}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r(x+p)=r(x)+\int_0^1J(x+tp)p\,dt,\quad M_k(p)=r(x_k)+J(x_k)p,\quad p_k=-J(x_k)^{-1}r(x_k)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-order residual model for nonlinear equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded derivation principle contrasting residual-system Newton modeling with scalar-objective Newton modeling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At an iterate $x_k$, Newton's method for nonlinear equations replaces each differentiable residual component $r_i(x_k+p)$ by the affine first-order model $$M_{k,i}(p)=r_i(x_k)+\nabla r_i(x_k)^Tp.$$ Thus the nonlinear-equation construction uses a linear residual model, whereas Newton's method for minimizing a smooth scalar objective is derived from a quadratic Taylor model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Newton's method for nonlinear equations forms an affine first-order model from the residual values and derivatives at the current iterate. This differs from optimization Newton, which is derived from a quadratic model of a scalar objective.
assumptions_latex: r_i\text{ is differentiable at }x_k\text{ for each residual component }i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M_{k,i}(p)=r_i(x_k)+\nabla r_i(x_k)^Tp

children.title: Square Regular Newton Systems
children.top_down_role: The classical locally nonsingular equation regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Square Regular Newton Systems
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a root with nonsingular Jacobian and locally Lipschitz derivative, Newton steps are uniquely defined and converge quadratically from sufficiently close initial points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood \(U\) of \(x_*\), with \(F(x_*)=0\) and \(J_*:=F'(x_*)\) nonsingular. Suppose \(F'\) is Lipschitz continuous near \(x_*\). Then there exists a neighborhood \(V\subseteq U\) such that, for every \(x_0\in V\), the Newton systems \(F'(x_k)d_k=-F(x_k)\) have unique solutions, the iterates \(x_{k+1}=x_k+d_k\) remain in \(V\), and \(x_k\to x_*\). Moreover, for some \(C>0\), \[\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|\le C\|x_k-x_*\|^2\] whenever \(x_k\in V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_k\to x_*\) locally and \(\|x_{k+1}-x_*\|\le C\|x_k-x_*\|^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local quadratic convergence for a square nonlinear system at a regular root.

notation.meaning: Jacobian of F at the root x_*

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Square regular Newton system
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuously differentiable on an open set, and let \(x_*\in\mathcal D\) satisfy \(F(x_*)=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The classical locally nonsingular square-equation regime in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The root \(x_*\) is regular, or nondegenerate, when \[\det J_F(x_*)\ne0,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \operatorname{rank}J_F(x_*)=n.\] A Newton system \(J_F(x)p=-F(x)\) is square regular at \(x\) when \(J_F(x)\) is nonsingular. It is locally square regular about \(x_*\) when there exists a neighborhood \(U\subseteq\mathcal D\) of \(x_*\) such that \(J_F(x)\) is nonsingular for every \(x\in U\). In this regime the correction and update are uniquely defined by \[p_N(x)=-J_F(x)^{-1}F(x),\qquad N_F(x)=x+p_N(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A square nonlinear-equation root is regular when its square Jacobian has full rank. A Newton system is regular at a current point when that Jacobian is invertible, and it is locally regular around a root when invertibility persists throughout some neighborhood. In that regime the Newton correction is unique and equals the inverse-Jacobian action on the negative residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[J_F(x)\text{ nonsingular}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\{p:J_F(x)p=-F(x)\}=\{-J_F(x)^{-1}F(x)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a square matrix, \(\det J_F(x_*)\ne0\), \(\ker J_F(x_*)=\{0\}\), and \(\operatorname{rank}J_F(x_*)=n\) are equivalent.
The source terminology “nondegenerate solution” is the regular-root condition used here.
special_cases_latex: For a scalar equation, regularity is \(F'(x_*)\ne0\).
For the stationarity equation \(F=\nabla f\), regularity means that \(\nabla^2f(x_*)\) is nonsingular, without asserting positive definiteness.
immediate_consequences_latex: Continuity of \(J_F\) and nonsingularity at \(x_*\) imply nonsingularity throughout some sufficiently small neighborhood.
Every Newton system in that neighborhood has a unique exact correction.
boundary_notes: Regularity does not by itself imply that a remote starting point converges to the selected root.
A nonsingular but poorly conditioned Jacobian is mathematically regular but may be numerically unreliable.

notation.meaning: Unique Newton correction in the regular regime.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Singular, nonisolated, and multiple-root regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuously differentiable and let \(\mathcal Z=\{x\in\mathcal D:F(x)=0\}\). Fix \(x_*\in\mathcal Z\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A classification of finite-dimensional square roots by local Jacobian rank and local geometry of the zero set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The root \(x_*\) is singular or degenerate when \[\operatorname{rank}J_F(x_*)<n.\] It is nonisolated when every neighborhood \(U\) of \(x_*\) contains a distinct root, equivalently \[(U\cap\mathcal Z)\setminus\{x_*\}\ne\varnothing\quad\text{for every neighborhood }U.\] In the scalar case \(F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\), a root has multiplicity \(r\ge2\) when \(F\) is \(r\)-times differentiable near \(x_*\) and \[F(x_*)=F'(x_*)=\cdots=F^{(r-1)}(x_*)=0,\qquad F^{(r)}(x_*)\ne0.\] A singular-root geometry regime is any local Newton problem satisfying at least one of these conditions; the conditions are related but not equivalent in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A square root is singular when the Jacobian at the root is rank deficient. It is nonisolated when other roots occur arbitrarily close to it. For a scalar smooth equation, a multiple root is characterized by the vanishing of all derivatives below its multiplicity and a nonzero derivative at the multiplicity order. These categories overlap, but singularity alone neither forces a continuum of roots nor supplies a scalar multiplicity notion in several dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x_*\text{ lies in a singular-root geometry regime}\iff \operatorname{rank}J_F(x_*)<n\ \text{or}\ x_*\text{ is nonisolated}\ \text{or, for }n=1,\ x_*\text{ has multiplicity }r\ge2.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a square system, singularity is equivalent to \(\ker J_F(x_*)\ne\{0\}\).
Nonisolation is equivalent to the existence of a sequence \(x_j\in\mathcal Z\setminus\{x_*\}\) with \(x_j\to x_*\).
special_cases_latex: The scalar residual \(F(x)=x^r\) has a root of multiplicity \(r\) at zero and \(F'(0)=0\) for \(r\ge2\).
A smooth zero manifold of positive local dimension consists entirely of nonisolated roots, typically with rank-deficient square Jacobians.
immediate_consequences_latex: At a singular root, the classical inverse formula \(-J_F(x_*)^{-1}F(x_*)\) is unavailable.
A nonisolated root cannot be uniquely selected by the equation \(F(x)=0\) within any neighborhood.
boundary_notes: Multivariate multiplicity requires additional algebraic or analytic structure and is not defined by the scalar derivative test.
A singular root may still be isolated, and a rank-deficient Newton equation away from the root may be inconsistent or nonunique.

notation.meaning: Zero set of the nonlinear map.

review_flags: The inspected source explicitly supports degenerate roots and the scalar multiple-root example, but no single inspected locator supports the full combined definition including nonisolated-root geometry and the stated scalar multiplicity criterion.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular, nonisolated, and multiple-root regimes
Singular Jacobian Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular Jacobian yields an exact Newton step only when the residual lies in its range, and any such step is nonunique along the null space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F:U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), the Newton correction at \(x\in U\) is any solution of \(Jd=-F(x)\), where \(J:=F'(x)\). If \(J\) is singular, a correction exists exactly when \(F(x)\in\operatorname{range}(J)\). When it exists, it is nonunique whenever \(\ker(J)\ne\{0\}\): every correction has the form \(d=d_0+z\) with \(z\in\ker(J)\). Thus singularity removes the classical unique-step guarantee; if \(F(x)\notin\operatorname{range}(J)\), the exact Newton equation is inconsistent and requires a generalized, projected, or regularized replacement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Jd=-F(x)\) is solvable iff \(F(x)\in\operatorname{range}(J)\), and its solution is not unique when \(\ker(J)\ne\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solvability and uniqueness boundary for Newton corrections at rank-deficient Jacobians.

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.2.4. The null space p. 22

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shifted normal-equation regularization and its parameter tradeoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded Levenberg–Marquardt-type regularization for Newton steps in nonlinear equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\lambda_k>0\), define \(p_k=-(J_k^TJ_k+\lambda_kI)^{-1}J_k^Tr_k\). Then \(J_k^TJ_k+\lambda_kI\) is nonsingular; if \(\lambda_k\) is bounded away from zero, the resulting directions satisfy a uniform positive-angle condition of the form \(\cos\theta_k\ge\delta>0\). The system can be factored without explicitly forming \(J_k^TJ_k\): if the stacked matrix \(\begin{bmatrix}J_k\\ \sqrt\lambda I\end{bmatrix}\) has upper-triangular QR factor \(R\), then \(R^TR=J_k^TJ_k+\lambda I\). As \(\lambda_k\to\infty\), \(p_k\sim-\lambda_k^{-1}J_k^Tr_k\), producing a small steepest-descent-like step and potentially losing Newton's fast local rate; values that are too small may be inefficient near singular Jacobians.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive identity shift makes the normal-equation Newton matrix nonsingular and, when kept away from zero, controls the direction angle. A stacked QR factorization implements the shift without forming the normal matrix. Excessively large shifts reduce the method to small gradient-like steps, while excessively small shifts give poor protection near singular Jacobians.
assumptions_latex: For the factorization identity, \(\begin{bmatrix}J_k\\ \sqrt\lambda I\end{bmatrix}=QR\) with \(R\) upper triangular
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J_k^TJ_k+\lambda_kI\) is nonsingular, the shifted step is \(p_k=-(J_k^TJ_k+\lambda_kI)^{-1}J_k^Tr_k\), and \(R^TR=J_k^TJ_k+\lambda I\); large and small shifts have the stated convergence-speed and singularity-protection boundaries.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonisolated Root Manifolds
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under constant rank, nearby roots form a manifold whose tangent space is the Jacobian null space; Newton linearization cannot select motion along that manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable, let \(F(x_*)=0\), and suppose \(F'\) has constant rank \(r\) on a neighborhood of \(x_*\). Then the local zero set \(M:=\{x\in U:F(x)=0\}\) is, near \(x_*\), an embedded submanifold of dimension \(n-r\), with tangent space \[T_{x_*}M=\ker F'(x_*).\] Consequently, when \(r<n\), the root is nonisolated. A linearized equation determines only the component transverse to \(T_{x_*}M\); tangent components remain free unless an additional selection rule, such as minimum norm or orthogonality, is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is locally an \((n-r)\)-dimensional manifold and \(T_{x_*}M=\ker F'(x_*)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-rank geometry of a locally nonisolated nonlinear-equation solution set.

notation.meaning: tangent space of M at x_*

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The constant-rank manifold statement is mathematically standard and fits the leaf, but no citation is supplied for the manifold dimension, tangent-space identity, or nonisolated-root conclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Root Behavior
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a scalar root of multiplicity m at least two, ordinary Newton iteration converges locally linearly with asymptotic factor (m−1)/m. Multiplying the Newton correction by m yields local quadratic convergence under the stated regularity assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) be an open interval containing \(x_*\), and let \(f:I\to\mathbb{R}\) admit the factorization \(f(x)=(x-x_*)^m g(x)\), where \(m\ge 2\), \(g\in C^2(I)\), and \(g(x_*)\ne 0\). For the unmodified Newton iteration \(x_{k+1}=x_k-f(x_k)/f'(x_k)\), define \(e_k:=x_k-x_*\). For iterates sufficiently close to but distinct from \(x_*\), \[e_{k+1}=\frac{m-1}{m}e_k+O(e_k^2).\] Thus the local convergence is linear with asymptotic factor \((m-1)/m\). If \(m\) is known, the modified iteration \(x_{k+1}=x_k-m f(x_k)/f'(x_k)\) instead satisfies \(e_{k+1}=O(e_k^2)\) for iterates sufficiently close to \(x_*\).
assumptions_latex: The iterates are sufficiently close to \(x_*\), with divisions evaluated only where \(f'(x_k)\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For ordinary Newton iteration, \(e_{k+1}=((m-1)/m)e_k+O(e_k^2)\); for the multiplicity-corrected iteration, \(e_{k+1}=O(e_k^2)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Restoration Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full rank arbitrarily near a singular root is insufficient for stability: the inverse Jacobian diverges unless the smallest singular value is uniformly bounded away from zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be nonsingular Jacobians converging to a singular matrix \(J_*\). Then \(\sigma_{\min}(J_k)\to0\) and \(\|J_k^{-1}\|_2=1/\sigma_{\min}(J_k)\to\infty\). Therefore pointwise restoration of full rank near a singular root does not provide a uniformly stable Newton regime. For equations \(J_kd_k=-F(x_k)\), residual components aligned with a left singular vector associated with \(\sigma_{\min}(J_k)\) can produce corrections of order \(\|F(x_k)\|/\sigma_{\min}(J_k)\). Uniform regular-step bounds are recovered only on regions where \(\sigma_{\min}(J(x))\ge\gamma>0\).
assumptions_latex: \(J_k\to J_*\), each \(J_k\) is nonsingular, and \(J_*\) is singular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{\min}(J_k)\to0\) and \(\|J_k^{-1}\|_2\to\infty\); uniform stability requires \(\sigma_{\min}(J(x))\ge\gamma>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditioning boundary between rank-deficient and uniformly regular Newton systems.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The conditioning boundary is mathematically plausible and failure_boundary is the correct role, but no source supports the singular-value limit, inverse-norm identity, or uniform stability characterization.

children.title: Rectangular-System Interface
children.top_down_role: Projected and generalized Newton interpretations for nonsquare systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Rectangular-System Interface
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonsquare system, the pseudoinverse Newton step minimizes the linearized residual and selects the minimum-norm correction, with familiar full-rank formulas in both orientations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be differentiable at \(x\), with \(J:=F'(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\). The canonical generalized Newton correction is \[d=-J^\dagger F(x),\] where \(J^\dagger\) is the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse. Equivalently, \(d\) minimizes \(\|Jd+F(x)\|_2\) and, among all residual-minimizing corrections, has minimum Euclidean norm. If \(m\ge n\) and \(J\) has full column rank, then \(d=-(J^TJ)^{-1}J^TF(x)\). If \(m\le n\) and \(J\) has full row rank, then \(d=-J^T(JJ^T)^{-1}F(x)\).
assumptions_latex: \(J=F'(x)\) has the stated full-rank property when an explicit inverse formula is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d=-J^\dagger F(x)\) is the minimum-norm minimizer of \(\|Jd+F(x)\|_2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moore–Penrose projected Newton correction for nonsquare nonlinear systems.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The pseudoinverse characterization and both full-rank formulas are correct, and representation fits the leaf. The cited Gauss–Newton locator may support the overdetermined full-column-rank case but does not establish support for the general minimum-norm characterization and underdetermined full-row-rank formula.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rectangular generalized Newton interface
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable, where possibly \(m\ne n\), and let \(J=J_F(x)\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonsquare systems represented through least-squares or minimum-norm solutions of the affine residual equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The rectangular Newton interface at \(x\) is the affine model \[M_x(p)=F(x)+Jp.\] If \(m\ge n\), a least-squares generalized Newton correction is any \[p\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{v\in\mathbb R^n}\|F(x)+Jv\|_2,\] and, when \(J\) has full column rank, it is uniquely characterized by \[J^TJp=-J^TF(x),\qquad p=-J^+F(x).\] For arbitrary rank, the canonical minimum-norm least-squares correction is \[p=-J^+F(x),\] where \(J^+\) is the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse. If the affine equation \(Jp=-F(x)\) is consistent and underdetermined, this choice is the solution having minimum Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonsquare residual map, the affine model remains the basic Newton object, but setting it to zero may be impossible or may leave many corrections. The rectangular interface therefore selects a correction by minimizing the affine residual, with minimum Euclidean norm used to remove nonuniqueness. The Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse expresses this canonical choice. In the full-column-rank overdetermined case, the correction is equivalently characterized by the normal equations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[p_{\mathrm{GN}}(x)=-J_F(x)^+F(x)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{p}\|F(x)+J_F(x)p\|_2,\] with minimum \(\|p\|_2\) among all least-squares minimizers.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Under full column rank, \(p=-J^+F\) is equivalent to \((J^TJ)p=-J^TF\).
If \(-F\in\operatorname{range}(J)\), the least-squares residual is zero and the pseudoinverse selects the minimum-norm exact solution.
special_cases_latex: When \(m=n\) and \(J\) is nonsingular, \(J^+=J^{-1}\), recovering the classical Newton correction.
For \(m>n\) with full column rank, the interface is the Gauss-Newton correction for minimizing \(\tfrac12\|F(x)\|_2^2\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The predicted residual \(F(x)+Jp\) is orthogonal to \(\operatorname{range}(J)\) at every least-squares correction.
Rank deficiency does not prevent definition of the pseudoinverse correction, although it may make the correction sensitive.
boundary_notes: The normal equations should not be interpreted as requiring their explicit numerical formation.
Weighted norms, regularization, and alternative generalized inverses define different interfaces.

notation.meaning: Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of the rectangular Jacobian.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unconstrained Newton stationarity and model representations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable, and fix \(x\in\mathcal D\). Set \(g=\nabla f(x)\) and \(H=\nabla^2f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-Hessian, finite-dimensional unconstrained Newton models; positive definiteness is not assumed unless a model minimizer is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The unconstrained Newton model at \(x\) is \[m_x(p)=f(x)+g^Tp+	frac12p^THp.\] A Newton correction is any \(p\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfying the model-stationarity equation \[
abla_pm_x(p)=g+Hp=0.\] Equivalently, it is a Newton correction for the nonlinear stationarity equation \(
abla f(x)=0\), because the Jacobian of \(
abla f\) is \(H\). If \(H\) is nonsingular, the correction is unique and equals \(p_N=-H^{-1}g\). If \(H\succ0\), this stationary point is the unique global minimizer of \(m_x\); if \(H\) is indefinite, the equation may still have a unique solution, but that solution is not a model minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unconstrained Newton model is the second-order Taylor model at the current point. Its stationary points solve the Newton linear system. This is the same system obtained by applying equation-solving Newton to the gradient equation. Nonsingularity of the Hessian gives a unique stationary correction, while positive definiteness is the stronger condition that makes this correction the unique minimizer of the quadratic model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\{p:\nabla_pm_x(p)=0\}=\{p:Hp=-g\},\] and if \(H\) is nonsingular this set is \(\{-H^{-1}g\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The stationarity residual representation uses \(F=\nabla f\) and \(J_F=\nabla^2f\).
When \(H\succ0\), \(p_N=\operatorname*{argmin}_{p\in\mathbb R^n}m_x(p)\).
special_cases_latex: For a quadratic objective, the model differs from the objective at \(x+p\) only by an irrelevant exact identity of coordinates.
At a stationary point \(g=0\), \(p=0\) satisfies the Newton equation.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(H\succ0\) and \(g\ne0\), then \(g^Tp_N=-p_N^THp_N<0\), so the Newton correction is a descent direction.
If \(H\) is singular, the model-stationarity equation may have no solution or multiple solutions.
boundary_notes: A local quadratic model need not approximate the objective well for a large step.
Nonsmooth objectives require generalized derivatives and are outside this definition.

notation.meaning: Gradient of the objective at the current point.
Exact Hessian at the current point.

knowledge_statements.title: Stationarity-Equation View
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimization Newton steps are precisely Newton steps for the gradient equation; they target any stationary point unless curvature or globalization conditions enforce minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}\) be twice continuously differentiable. First-order stationary points solve the nonlinear equation \(G(x):=
abla f(x)=0\), whose Jacobian is \(G'(x)=
abla^2 f(x)\). Hence Newton's method applied to stationarity computes \(d_k\) from \[
abla^2 f(x_k)d_k=-
abla f(x_k)\] and sets \(x_{k+1}=x_k+d_k\). If \(
abla^2 f(x_k)\) is nonsingular, the correction is unique. This equation-solving representation targets stationary points; without positive-definiteness or globalization assumptions, it does not distinguish local minimizers from maximizers or saddle points.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable on an open set \(U\).
\(\nabla^2 f(x_k)\) is nonsingular when uniqueness is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_k\) satisfies \(\nabla^2 f(x_k)d_k=-\nabla f(x_k)\), followed by \(x_{k+1}=x_k+d_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained Newton optimization represented as Newton's method for the gradient equation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The equation-solving interpretation of exact Newton corrections for smooth unconstrained optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The stationarity-equation view defines an unconstrained optimization Newton correction at \(x\) as a Newton correction for \[G(x)=
abla f(x)=0.\] Since \(J_G(x)=
abla^2f(x)\), its affine model is \[G(x)+J_G(x)p=
abla f(x)+
abla^2f(x)p.\] Hence \(p\) is a stationarity-equation Newton correction precisely when \[
abla^2f(x)p=-
abla f(x).\] This definition targets a stationary point. It does not, without a curvature condition, distinguish a local minimizer from a local maximizer or saddle point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stationarity-equation view, minimizing a smooth unconstrained objective is locally represented as solving its gradient equation. Newton linearizes the gradient residual, whose Jacobian is the Hessian, and chooses a correction that zeros this affine model. The resulting equation identifies stationary points rather than minima specifically; the type of stationary point must be determined from curvature or other information.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\[p	ext{ is a Newton correction for }G=
abla f\iff 
abla^2f(x)p=-
abla f(x).\]

When \(
abla^2f(x)\) is invertible, \(p=-
abla^2f(x)^{-1}
abla f(x)\).
The equation is identical to the first-order stationarity condition of the exact-Hessian quadratic model.
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is a strictly convex quadratic, the stationarity equation is linear and one full Newton correction reaches its unique minimizer.
At any stationary point, the zero correction solves the linearized stationarity equation.
immediate_consequences_latex: A nonsingular Hessian makes the stationarity correction unique.
An invertible indefinite Hessian still defines a correction even though the represented stationary point need not be a minimum.
boundary_notes: First-order stationarity is necessary but generally not sufficient for local optimality.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-Model View
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Newton equation is the stationarity condition of the second-order Taylor model; positive-definite Hessian makes its solution the unique model minimizer and a descent direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For twice differentiable \(f:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}\), define at \(x_k\) the quadratic model \[m_k(d)=f(x_k)+g_k^Td+	frac12 d^TH_kd,\qquad g_k:=
abla f(x_k),\quad H_k:=
abla^2f(x_k).\] Its stationarity equation is \(H_kd=-g_k\), exactly the Newton equation. If \(H_k\succ0\), the unique Newton correction \(d_k=-H_k^{-1}g_k\) is the unique global minimizer of \(m_k\), and \(g_k^Td_k<0\) whenever \(g_k
e0\). If \(H_k\) is merely nonsingular, the Newton correction remains the model's unique stationary point but need not minimize it.
assumptions_latex: \(H_k\) is nonsingular, and positive definite when minimization is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H_kd_k=-g_k\); if \(H_k\succ0\), then \(d_k\) uniquely minimizes \(m_k\) and is a descent direction for \(g_k\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Newton correction as the stationary point or minimizer of a local quadratic model.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact-Hessian quadratic Newton model
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable. Fix \(x\in\mathcal D\), and write \(g=\nabla f(x)\) and \(H=\nabla^2f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An unconstrained local second-order model; unrestricted minimization is asserted only under positive-definite curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The quadratic-model representation of the objective at \(x\) is \[m_x(p)=f(x)+g^Tp+\tfrac12p^THp,\qquad p\in\mathbb R^n.\] A quadratic-model Newton correction is a stationary point of this model, so it satisfies \[\nabla_pm_x(p)=g+Hp=0.\] If \(H\succ0\), the model is strictly convex and the correction is defined equivalently by \[p_N=\operatorname*{argmin}_{p\in\mathbb R^n}m_x(p)=-H^{-1}g.\] If \(H\succeq0\) is singular, a minimizer exists exactly when \(g\in\operatorname{range}(H)\), and it need not be unique. For indefinite \(H\), the unrestricted model is unbounded below despite possibly having a stationary Newton correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quadratic-model view represents the objective near the current point by its exact second-order Taylor polynomial in the step. A Newton correction is a stationary point of that polynomial. When the Hessian is positive definite, this point is its unique unrestricted minimizer. Singular positive-semidefinite curvature may produce no stationary point or many minimizers, while indefinite curvature makes the unrestricted model unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\nabla_pm_x(p)=0\iff Hp=-g,\] and under \(H\succ0\), \[p_N=-H^{-1}g=\operatorname*{argmin}_{p}m_x(p).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The first-order condition of the model is the Newton equation for the stationarity residual \(\nabla f\).
Adding or removing the constant term \(f(x)\) does not change the model correction.
special_cases_latex: If \(H=I\), the model correction is the negative gradient \(p_N=-g\).
For a quadratic objective with constant Hessian, \(m_x(p)=f(x+p)\) exactly.
immediate_consequences_latex: Under positive definiteness, the model reduction at the Newton correction is \(m_x(0)-m_x(p_N)=\tfrac12p_N^THp_N\).
Negative curvature prevents an unrestricted model minimizer and motivates a trust-region or Hessian modification.
boundary_notes: The model is local and its minimizer need not decrease the true objective without step control.
Quasi-Newton models replace \(H\) by an approximation and are not the exact-Hessian definition here.

notation.meaning: Exact second-order Taylor model as a function of the step.
The Hessian is symmetric positive definite.

knowledge_statements.title: Indefinite Newton-Model Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With an indefinite Hessian, the quadratic model is unbounded below, and its Newton stationary point is a saddle that may fail to be a descent direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m(d)=f+g^Td+\tfrac12d^THd\), where \(H=H^T\) is nonsingular but indefinite. If \(v^THv<0\) for some \(v\ne0\), then \(m(tv)\to-\infty\) along one of the rays \(t\to\pm\infty\); thus the unconstrained model has no global minimizer. The Newton correction \(d_N=-H^{-1}g\) is its unique stationary point, but it is a saddle point of \(m\). Moreover, \(g^Td_N=-g^TH^{-1}g\) need not be negative, so \(d_N\) need not be a descent direction for the objective. A trust region, line-search modification, or curvature regularization is therefore required to enforce minimization behavior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m\) is unbounded below, \(d_N=-H^{-1}g\) is a saddle point, and \(g^Td_N<0\) is not guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Negative-curvature failure of the unconstrained quadratic Newton model.

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.2 Newton's Method p. 51

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Indefinite and negative-curvature Newton geometry
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(m(p)=m(0)+g^Tp+\tfrac12p^THp\) with \(H=H^T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unrestricted smooth quadratic models with an indefinite exact Hessian; trust-region regularization is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Newton model has indefinite geometry when \(H\) has at least one positive and at least one negative eigenvalue. A nonzero vector \(d\) is a negative-curvature direction when \[d^THd<0.\] If \(H\) is nonsingular, the Newton stationary correction is \(p_N=-H^{-1}g\), but its model Hessian remains indefinite, so \(p_N\) is a saddle point of \(m\), not a local minimizer. Moreover, for every negative-curvature direction \(d\), \[m(p_N+td)=m(p_N)+\tfrac12t^2d^THd\to-\infty\quad\text{as }|t|\to\infty.\] Thus an indefinite unrestricted Newton model has no global minimizer even when its Newton equation has a unique solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Newton quadratic model is indefinite when its symmetric Hessian has eigenvalues of both signs. Any direction with a negative quadratic form is a negative-curvature direction. An invertible indefinite Hessian still yields a unique stationary Newton correction, but that correction is a saddle of the model, and the model decreases without bound along every negative-curvature direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[H\text{ indefinite}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \inf_{p\in\mathbb R^n}m(p)=-\infty,\] while nonsingularity additionally gives the unique stationary point \(p_N=-H^{-1}g\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For symmetric \(H\), negative curvature exists exactly when \(\lambda_{\min}(H)<0\).
Indefiniteness is equivalent to \(\lambda_{\min}(H)<0<\lambda_{\max}(H)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(g=0\) and \(H\) is indefinite, the origin is a stationary saddle of the model.
A negative-definite Hessian gives a strict model maximizer rather than an indefinite saddle, but the model is still unbounded below.
immediate_consequences_latex: The Newton correction need not be a descent direction for the original objective when the Hessian is indefinite.
A bounded step subproblem or curvature modification is required to define a model minimizer.
boundary_notes: A singular Hessian with a negative eigenvalue is also unbounded below but may lack a unique stationary point.
This definition classifies the model, not the global geometry of the nonlinear objective.

notation.meaning: A candidate direction of negative curvature.
Smallest eigenvalue of the symmetric Hessian.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full-space and reduced-space equality Newton representations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(c(x)=0\), with \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) and \(c:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) twice continuously differentiable. Let \(\mathcal L(x,\lambda)=f(x)-\lambda^Tc(x)\), \(A=J_c(x)\), \(g_L=\nabla_x\mathcal L(x,\lambda)\), and \(H_L=\nabla_{xx}^2\mathcal L(x,\lambda)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional equality constraints, exact Lagrangian Hessian, and local linearized feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The full-space equality-constrained Newton correction \((p,p_\lambda)\) solves \[\begin{bmatrix}H_L&-A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}p\\p_\lambda\end{bmatrix}=-\begin{bmatrix}g_L\\c(x)\end{bmatrix}.\] If \(A\) has full row rank, choose \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-m)}\) with \(AZ=0\) and full column rank, and choose a particular normal correction \(p_Y\) satisfying \(Ap_Y=-c(x)\). Writing \(p=p_Y+Zq\), the reduced-space representation is \[(Z^TH_LZ)q=-Z^T(g_L+H_Lp_Y).\] When \(Z^TH_LZ\) is nonsingular, the reduced correction and the full KKT correction determine the same primal step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equality-constrained Newton systems admit a coupled primal-dual representation and a tangent-space representation. The coupled form linearizes Lagrangian stationarity and feasibility simultaneously. The reduced form first chooses a correction that restores linearized feasibility, then determines the remaining tangent component with the reduced Hessian. Under full row rank and nonsingular reduced curvature, both forms define the same primal correction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[p=p_Y+Zq,\quad Ap_Y=-c(x),\quad (Z^TH_LZ)q=-Z^T(g_L+H_Lp_Y)\] is the reduced representation of the displayed full Newton-KKT system.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The full system is Newton's method applied to \((\nabla_x\mathcal L,c)=0\).
The same primal step is the stationary point of \(g_L^Tp+\tfrac12p^TH_Lp\) subject to \(Ap+c(x)=0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Full KKT Newton System
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equality-constrained Newton simultaneously linearizes stationarity and feasibility, producing a coupled saddle-point system for the primal and multiplier corrections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_x f(x)\) subject to \(c(x)=0\), where \(c:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), and define \(L(x,\lambda):=f(x)+\lambda^Tc(x)\). At \((x_k,\lambda_k)\), let \(H_k:=\nabla_{xx}^2L(x_k,\lambda_k)\), \(A_k:=c'(x_k)\), and \(g_k:=\nabla_xL(x_k,\lambda_k)\). Newton's method for the KKT equations computes \((p_k,\delta\lambda_k)\) from \[\begin{pmatrix}H_k&A_k^T\\A_k&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}p_k\\\delta\lambda_k\end{pmatrix}=-\begin{pmatrix}g_k\\c(x_k)\end{pmatrix},\] then sets \(x_{k+1}=x_k+p_k\) and \(\lambda_{k+1}=\lambda_k+\delta\lambda_k\).
assumptions_latex: \(A_k\) has full row rank and \(H_k\) is positive definite on \(\ker A_k\) when nonsingularity is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The primal-dual Newton correction solves the displayed KKT saddle-point system.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coupled Newton linearization of equality-constrained first-order optimality equations.

notation.meaning: Lagrangian Hessian with respect to x

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coupled primal-dual KKT Newton system
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(c(x)=0\), define \(\mathcal L(x,\lambda)=f(x)-\lambda^Tc(x)\), \(A(x)=J_c(x)\), and \(R(x,\lambda)=(\nabla_x\mathcal L(x,\lambda),c(x))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Newton linearization of the smooth equality-constrained KKT residual in the full primal-dual space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a primal-dual point \((x,\lambda)\), the full KKT Newton system is \[J_R(x,\lambda)\begin{bmatrix}p\\p_\lambda\end{bmatrix}=-R(x,\lambda),\] namely \[\begin{bmatrix}\nabla_{xx}^2\mathcal L(x,\lambda)&-A(x)^T\\A(x)&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}p\\p_\lambda\end{bmatrix}=-\begin{bmatrix}\nabla_x\mathcal L(x,\lambda)\\c(x)\end{bmatrix}.\] The primal block enforces stationarity of the affine KKT model, and the constraint block enforces linearized feasibility \(A(x)p+c(x)=0\). A full Newton update is \((x^+,\lambda^+)=(x+p,\lambda+p_\lambda)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The full KKT Newton system is the Jacobian equation obtained by applying Newton's method to the coupled residual formed by Lagrangian stationarity and equality feasibility. Its unknowns are both the primal correction and the multiplier correction. The second block row imposes linearized feasibility, while the first block row corrects stationarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\begin{bmatrix}p\\p_\lambda\end{bmatrix}\in\left\{v:J_R(x,\lambda)v=-R(x,\lambda)\right\},\qquad (x^+,\lambda^+)=(x+p,\lambda+p_\lambda).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Replacing \(p_\lambda\) by \(\lambda^+-\lambda\) gives the SQP KKT system with the next multiplier \(\lambda^+\) as an unknown.
The primal correction solves the stationarity conditions of the quadratic Lagrangian model subject to the linearized equality constraints.
special_cases_latex: At a feasible point, the second block row reduces to \(A(x)p=0\).
With no equality constraints, the first block row is the unconstrained Newton equation.
immediate_consequences_latex: Full row rank of \(A\) and nonsingularity of the reduced Hessian imply uniqueness of both corrections.
The KKT coefficient matrix is symmetric under the displayed sign convention after a harmless sign change of the multiplier variable.
boundary_notes: An indefinite KKT matrix is normal even when reduced curvature is positive definite.
Inequality KKT systems additionally contain slack, sign, and complementarity blocks.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full Newton System for Equality-Constrained KKT Equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact primal-dual Newton representation for a smooth equality-constrained nonlinear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n} f(x)\) subject to \(c(x)=0\), let \(\mathcal L(x,\lambda)=f(x)-\lambda^Tc(x)\) and let \(A(x)\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) satisfy \(A(x)^T=[\nabla c_1(x),\ldots,\nabla c_m(x)]\). The KKT residual and its Jacobian are
\[
F(x,\lambda)=\begin{bmatrix}\nabla f(x)-A(x)^T\lambda\\c(x)\end{bmatrix},\qquad
F'(x,\lambda)=\begin{bmatrix}\nabla^2_{xx}\mathcal L(x,\lambda)&-A(x)^T\\A(x)&0\end{bmatrix}.
\]
At \((x_k,\lambda_k)\), the Newton correction \((p_k,p_\lambda)\) solves
\[
\begin{bmatrix}\nabla^2_{xx}\mathcal L_k&-A_k^T\\A_k&0\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}p_k\\p_\lambda\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}-\nabla f_k+A_k^T\lambda_k\\-c_k\end{bmatrix},
\]
and \((x_{k+1},\lambda_{k+1})=(x_k+p_k,\lambda_k+p_\lambda)\). This iteration is well defined whenever the displayed KKT matrix is nonsingular. Moreover, any local solution \(x^*\) at which \(A(x^*)\) has full row rank admits a multiplier \(\lambda^*\) satisfying \(F(x^*,\lambda^*)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth equality-constrained problem, the KKT stationarity and feasibility equations form a nonlinear primal-dual system. Newton's method applied to that system produces the full saddle-point KKT linear system for the primal and multiplier corrections. The correction is uniquely defined when its KKT matrix is nonsingular, and a local solution with full-row-rank constraint Jacobian satisfies the KKT system for an appropriate multiplier.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\text{ and }c:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\text{ are smooth}
A(x^*)\text{ has full row rank for the stated necessary KKT condition}
\begin{bmatrix}\nabla^2_{xx}\mathcal L_k&-A_k^T\\A_k&0\end{bmatrix}\text{ is nonsingular for a unique Newton correction}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F'(x_k,\lambda_k)\begin{bmatrix}p_k\\p_\lambda\end{bmatrix}=-F(x_k,\lambda_k),\qquad (x_{k+1},\lambda_{k+1})=(x_k+p_k,\lambda_k+p_\lambda).

knowledge_statements.title: Null-Space Equality Method
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The null-space method first restores linearized feasibility, then solves a reduced Hessian system on the constraint tangent space and finally recovers the multiplier correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(H=H^T\), full-row-rank \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), residuals \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^m\), choose \(Z\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(n-m)}\) with \(AZ=0\) and choose \(Y\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\) so that \(AY\) is nonsingular. Compute \(q\) from \((AY)q=-c\), then compute \(w\) from \[(Z^THZ)w=-Z^T(g+HYq).\] Set \(p=Yq+Zw\), and recover \(\delta\lambda\) from \(A^T\delta\lambda=-(g+Hp)\). If \(Z^THZ\) is nonsingular, this output is the unique solution of the full KKT Newton system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((p,\delta\lambda)\) solves \(Hp+A^T\delta\lambda=-g\) and \(Ap=-c\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal tangent-space reduction of an equality-constrained Newton saddle-point system.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Null-space reduction of an equality Newton system
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(Hp+A^T\nu=-g\), \(Ap=-c\), where \(H=H^T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank, and \(m\le n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic tangent-space reduction of a full-row-rank equality-constrained Newton or quadratic-program KKT system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-m)}\) with full column rank and \(AZ=0\), and choose \(Y\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\) such that \([Y\mid Z]\) is nonsingular. Decompose \[p=Yp_Y+Zp_Z.\] The null-space method defines \(p_Y\) and \(p_Z\) successively by \[(AY)p_Y=-c,\] \[(Z^THZ)p_Z=-Z^T(g+HYp_Y).\] It then sets \(p=Yp_Y+Zp_Z\) and recovers \(\nu\) from \[A^T\nu=-(g+Hp).\] The first component restores linearized feasibility; the second lies in \(\ker A\) and optimizes stationarity within the tangent space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The null-space method decomposes the equality-constrained correction into a particular component that satisfies the linearized constraints and a tangential component lying in the null space of the constraint Jacobian. It solves first for feasibility and then solves a reduced system involving the reduced Hessian. The multiplier is recovered only after the primal correction has been assembled.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[p=Yp_Y+Zp_Z,\quad (AY)p_Y=-c,\quad (Z^THZ)p_Z=-Z^T(g+HYp_Y).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The tangential equation is obtained by projecting the primal KKT equation with \(Z^T\), which removes the multiplier term because \(AZ=0\).
When \(x\) is feasible, \(c=0\) permits \(p_Y=0\), so only the reduced tangent system remains.
special_cases_latex: If \(n-m\) is small, the reduced system has substantially lower dimension than the full KKT system.
With an orthonormal null-space basis, \(Z^THZ\) is the restriction of the quadratic form to the tangent space.
immediate_consequences_latex: Full row rank of \(A\) makes \(AY\) nonsingular for every valid complementary basis \([Y\mid Z]\).
If \(Z^THZ\) is nonsingular, the tangential coordinate is unique.
boundary_notes: The basis \(Z\) is not unique, although the exact primal correction is basis independent.
Rank-deficient constraints or singular reduced curvature require additional compatibility conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Range-Space Equality Method
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The range-space method eliminates the primal correction, solves a Schur-complement system in multiplier space, and then recovers the primal step by back-substitution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given the KKT equations \(Hp+A^T\delta\lambda=-g\) and \(Ap=-c\), assume \(H\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is nonsingular and \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has full row rank. Form the range-space Schur complement \(S:=AH^{-1}A^T\). Compute \(u:=H^{-1}g\), solve \[S\,\delta\lambda=c-Au,\] and recover \(p=-H^{-1}(g+A^T\delta\lambda)\). If \(S\) is nonsingular, the resulting pair is the unique solution of the full KKT system. When \(H\succ0\), \(S\succ0\), so the reduced multiplier equation is symmetric positive definite and has dimension \(m\).
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is nonsingular and \(A\) has full row rank.
\(S=AH^{-1}A^T\) is nonsingular; positive definiteness follows when \(H\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Schur-complement solve and back-substitution yield the unique KKT correction \((p,\delta\lambda)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier-space Schur-complement reduction of an equality-constrained Newton saddle-point system.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Range-space Schur-complement equality method
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider the equality KKT system \(Hp+A^T\nu=-g\), \(Ap=-c\), with \(H=H^T\succ0\) and \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) of full row rank.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier-space elimination for equality Newton systems with invertible positive-definite primal curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The range-space equality method eliminates the primal correction through \[p=-H^{-1}(g+A^T
u).\] Substitution into the constraint equation defines the multiplier-space Schur-complement system \[S
u=c-AH^{-1}g,\qquad S=AH^{-1}A^T.\] Since \(H\succ0\) and \(A\) has full row rank, \(S\succ0\), so \(
u\) is uniquely determined. The primal correction is then recovered by solving \[Hp=-(g+A^T
u).\] The method is called range-space because the constraint correction is expressed using vectors in \(\operatorname{range}(A^T)\) and the reduced system has multiplier-space dimension \(m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The range-space method eliminates the primal variable from the KKT system using the inverse action of the positive-definite Hessian. This produces a symmetric positive-definite Schur-complement equation in the multipliers. After solving that smaller constraint-space equation, the primal correction is recovered by a Hessian solve.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The coefficient \(AH^{-1}A^T\) is the Schur complement of \(H\) in the KKT matrix, up to the sign determined by the multiplier convention.
Block Gaussian elimination of the full KKT system yields the same two-stage equations.
special_cases_latex: If \(H\) is diagonal or block diagonal, the inverse actions needed to form or apply the Schur complement can be inexpensive.
The approach is attractive when \(m\ll n\), because the reduced system is \(m\)-dimensional.
immediate_consequences_latex: Under the stated assumptions, both multiplier and primal corrections are unique.
The Schur-complement system may be solved without explicitly forming \(H^{-1}\).
boundary_notes: The displayed method requires an invertible \(H\); the null-space method can remain applicable when \(H\) itself is singular.
Explicit formation of the Schur complement may lose sparsity or magnify conditioning difficulties.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split the equality-constrained Newton step into a constraint-correcting normal component and a null-space component obtained from the reduced Lagrangian Hessian.

abla c(x_k)^	op\). Compute a normal component \(p_k^Y=Y_kq_k\) from \(J_kY_kq_k=-c(x_k)\). With \(L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\lambda^	op c(x)\) and \(W_k=
abla_{xx}^2L(x_k,\lambda_k)\), solve \((Z_k^	op W_kZ_k)p_k^Z=-Z_k^	op(
abla f(x_k)+W_kp_k^Y)\), and set \(p_k=p_k^Y+Z_kp_k^Z\). Output \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\), where \(\alpha_k\in(0,1]\) is chosen by globalization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduced-gradient and reduced-curvature Newton method
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(c(x)=0\), and suppose \(A(x)=J_c(x)\) has full row rank. Let \(Z(x)\) have columns spanning \(\ker A(x)\), and define \(\mathcal L(x,\lambda)=f(x)-\lambda^Tc(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local equality-constrained Newton computation organized in tangent coordinates, especially at a feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a feasible point \(x\), the reduced gradient and reduced Hessian are \[g_R=Z^T
abla f(x),\qquad H_R=Z^T
abla_{xx}^2\mathcal L(x,\lambda)Z.\] A reduced-space Newton coordinate \(q\in\mathbb R^{n-m}\) satisfies \[H_Rq=-g_R,\] and the corresponding tangential primal correction is \(p_T=Zq\), for which \(A(x)p_T=0\). At an infeasible point, choose a normal correction \(p_N\) with \(A(x)p_N=-c(x)\) and define the corrected reduced equation \[H_Rq=-Z^T igl(
abla_x\mathcal L(x,\lambda)+
abla_{xx}^2\mathcal L(x,\lambda)p_N igr),\qquad p=p_N+Zq.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reduced-space Newton method expresses the free part of an equality-constrained correction in tangent coordinates. The reduced gradient is the objective or Lagrangian gradient projected into the null space of the constraint Jacobian, and the reduced Hessian is the Lagrangian Hessian restricted to that space. Newton's equation is solved in these lower-dimensional coordinates. If the current point is infeasible, a separate normal correction first supplies linearized feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[p=p_N+Zq,\quad A(x)p_N=-c(x),\quad H_Rq=-Z^T\bigl(\nabla_x\mathcal L+\nabla_{xx}^2\mathcal L\,p_N\bigr).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: At a feasible point, the method is Newton's method applied to the quadratic reduced objective in the tangent coordinates \(q\).
The reduced equation is the null-space projection of the primal row of the full KKT system.
special_cases_latex: If \(c(x)=0\), one may set \(p_N=0\), giving \(H_Rq=-g_R\).
If \(n-m=0\), there are no tangent coordinates and only the normal feasibility correction remains.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(H_R\) is nonsingular, the reduced coordinate is unique.
If \(H_R\succ0\), the tangential quadratic model has a unique minimizer.
boundary_notes: The reduced gradient depends on the chosen basis coordinates, but the represented tangent vector is invariant under exact basis changes.
Curvature of a nonlinear feasible manifold beyond the Lagrangian Hessian is already encoded locally through the multiplier-dependent Hessian.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Active-set and primal-dual complementarity representations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(c_E(x)=0\) and \(c_I(x)\ge0\). Introduce slacks \(s=c_I(x)\ge0\), equality multipliers \(y\), inequality multipliers \(z\ge0\), and \(S=\operatorname{diag}(s)\), \(Z=\operatorname{diag}(z)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional nonlinear programs represented either by an active equality set or by slack-variable complementarity equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The inequality KKT conditions admit two Newton-system representations. For a candidate active set \(\mathcal A\), the active-set representation imposes \[c_E(x)=0,\qquad c_i(x)=0\ (i\in\mathcal A),\qquad z_i=0\ (i\notin\mathcal A),\] and treats the selected constraints as equalities in a KKT Newton system. The primal-dual complementarity representation uses the residual \[R_0(x,s,y,z)=\begin{bmatrix}\nabla f(x)-A_E(x)^Ty-A_I(x)^Tz\\Sz\\c_E(x)\\c_I(x)-s\end{bmatrix}=0,\qquad s\ge0,\ z\ge0.\] Its perturbed interior form replaces \(Sz=0\) by \(Sz=\mu e\) with \(\mu>0\) and \(s,z>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inequality-constrained Newton systems can represent the combinatorial choice of binding constraints explicitly or encode it through complementarity. An active-set representation fixes a candidate collection of inequalities as equalities and sets inactive multipliers to zero. A primal-dual representation introduces nonnegative slacks and multipliers and couples them by componentwise complementarity. Interior representations replace zero complementarity by a positive perturbation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[s_i z_i=0,\ s_i\ge0,\ z_i\ge0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m_I)\] encodes the active/inactive alternative, while \(s_i z_i=\mu>0\) defines its perturbed primal-dual form.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Componentwise complementarity is equivalent to \(Sz=0\) together with \(s,z\ge0\).
Under a correctly identified strictly complementary active set, the active-set equality representation and the unperturbed primal-dual representation describe the same KKT point.
special_cases_latex: With no inequalities, the residual reduces to the equality-constrained KKT residual.
For \(\mu>0\), every component of \(s\) and \(z\) is positive and no inequality is exactly active in slack coordinates.
immediate_consequences_latex: At an unperturbed KKT point, \(s_i>0\) forces \(z_i=0\), while \(z_i>0\) forces \(s_i=0\).
Linearizing either representation produces a structured Newton system.
boundary_notes: Without strict complementarity, an active constraint can have zero multiplier, so the active/inactive classification is degenerate.
Nonsmooth complementarity reformulations are outside the smooth slack-variable representation used here.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A candidate active set converts selected inequalities into equalities, producing a saddle-point Newton system plus sign and inactivity checks.

With \(L_{\mathcal A}(x,\lambda,\mu_{\mathcal A})=f(x)+\lambda^	op c(x)+\mu_{\mathcal A}^	op g_{\mathcal A}(x)\), the active-set KKT equations are \(
abla_xL_{\mathcal A}=0\), \(c(x)=0\), and \(g_{\mathcal A}(x)=0\). Their Newton correction satisfies \[ egin{pmatrix}W&J_c^	op&J_{\mathcal A}^	op\J_c&0&0\J_{\mathcal A}&0&0\end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix}p\\Delta\lambda\\Delta\mu_{\mathcal A}\end{pmatrix}=- egin{pmatrix}
abla_xL_{\mathcal A}\c\g_{\mathcal A}\end{pmatrix}.\] Inactive multipliers are set to zero; validity additionally requires \(g_i(x)\le0\) for \(i
otin\mathcal A\) and \(\mu_{\mathcal A}\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Candidate-active-set KKT Newton representation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(c_i(x)=0\) for \(i\in\mathcal E\) and \(c_i(x)\ge0\) for \(i\in\mathcal I\). Let \(\mathcal W\subseteq\mathcal E\cup\mathcal I\) contain every equality index and a candidate subset of inequality indices.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A smooth local equality-system representation induced by a candidate working set; correctness of the active-set guess is not assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c_{\mathcal W}(x)\) collect the constraints indexed by \(\mathcal W\), let \(A_{\mathcal W}(x)=Jc_{\mathcal W}(x)\), and define \[\mathcal L_{\mathcal W}(x,\lambda_{\mathcal W})=f(x)-\lambda_{\mathcal W}^Tc_{\mathcal W}(x).\] The active-set KKT residual is \[R_{\mathcal W}(x,\lambda_{\mathcal W})=\begin{bmatrix}\nabla_x\mathcal L_{\mathcal W}(x,\lambda_{\mathcal W})\\c_{\mathcal W}(x)\end{bmatrix}.\] Its Newton correction solves \[\begin{bmatrix}\nabla_{xx}^2\mathcal L_{\mathcal W}&-A_{\mathcal W}^T\\A_{\mathcal W}&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}p\\p_\lambda\end{bmatrix}=-R_{\mathcal W}(x,\lambda_{\mathcal W}).\] Multipliers of inequalities outside \(\mathcal W\) are represented as zero. A solution represents a KKT point of the original inequality problem only if all omitted inequalities remain feasible and all active inequality multipliers have the required nonnegative sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A candidate active set converts selected inequalities into equalities and forms the ordinary equality-constrained KKT residual for that working set. Newton's method applied to this residual gives a coupled primal-multiplier system using only the selected constraint Jacobian. Inactive inequality multipliers are set to zero. The representation becomes valid for the original inequality problem only after checking feasibility of omitted constraints and the signs of selected inequality multipliers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\[R_{\mathcal W}=0,\ c_i(x)\ge0\ (i\notin\mathcal W),
\lambda_i\ge0\ (i\in\mathcal W\cap\mathcal I),
\lambda_i=0\ (i\notin\mathcal W)\] is the candidate-active-set KKT representation together with its validity conditions.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a quadratic model, the primal correction is the solution of an equality-constrained quadratic subproblem with constraints in \(\mathcal W\).
If the correct strictly complementary active set is selected, the representation is the equality subsystem of the full complementarity KKT conditions.
special_cases_latex: If \(\mathcal W=\mathcal E\), all inequalities are treated as inactive.
If \(\mathcal I=\varnothing\), the representation is exactly the full equality-constrained KKT Newton system.
immediate_consequences_latex: A blocking omitted constraint indicates that the current working set must be enlarged for a feasible active-set step.
A negative multiplier for a selected inequality violates dual feasibility and indicates that the constraint cannot certify KKT optimality in the current representation.
boundary_notes: Weakly active constraints with zero multipliers can make active-set identification nonunique.
The definition does not specify a rule for adding or dropping working-set indices.

children.title: Nonlinear Complementarity Condition
children.top_down_role: The complementarity interface connecting inequality stationarity with Newton equation models.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Complementarity Condition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inequality complementarity is equivalent to zeroing an NCP function applied to each multiplier and the corresponding nonnegative slack residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an inequality residual \(g(x)\le0\) with multiplier \(\mu\ge0\), complementarity is the componentwise condition \[\mu_i\ge0,\qquad -g_i(x)\ge0,\qquad \mu_i[-g_i(x)]=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).\] Let \(\phi:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) be an NCP function satisfying \(\phi(a,b)=0\) if and only if \(a\ge0\), \(b\ge0\), and \(ab=0\). Then complementarity is equivalently represented by the nonlinear equations \(\Phi_i(x,\mu)=\phi(\mu_i,-g_i(x))=0\) for all \(i\). For example, the Fischer--Burmeister function is \(\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(a,b)=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}-a-b\).
assumptions_latex: \(\phi\) has the stated NCP zero-set property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le\mu\perp-g(x)\ge0\) if and only if \(\Phi(x,\mu)=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KKT complementarity for inequalities and its nonlinear-equation encoding.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stationarity and Complementarity for One Inequality Constraint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order condition presented for a feasible solution of a single smooth inequality constraint written as c_1(x)\geq 0.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a solution $x^*$ of a problem with the inequality constraint $c_1(x)\geq 0$, the stated first-order conditions require a multiplier $\lambda_1^*\geq 0$ such that
\[
\nabla_x\mathcal L(x^*,\lambda_1^*)=0,\qquad \lambda_1^*c_1(x^*)=0,
\]
where $\mathcal L(x,\lambda_1)=f(x)-\lambda_1c_1(x)$. Consequently, $c_1(x^*)>0$ implies $\lambda_1^*=0$, while $\lambda_1^*>0$ implies that the constraint is active: $c_1(x^*)=0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For one inequality constraint, stationarity is paired with a nonnegative multiplier and complementary slackness. An inactive constraint must have zero multiplier, and a strictly positive multiplier is possible only for an active constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nabla_x\mathcal L(x^*,\lambda_1^*)=0,\qquad \lambda_1^*c_1(x^*)=0;\qquad c_1(x^*)>0\Rightarrow\lambda_1^*=0,\quad \lambda_1^*>0\Rightarrow c_1(x^*)=0.

children.top_down_role: Perturbed complementarity representations used by barrier Newton methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbed Primal-Dual KKT Systems
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Barrier Newton methods replace zero complementarity by positive products of slacks and multipliers, then solve the coupled perturbed KKT equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimizing \(f(x)\) subject to \(c(x)=0\) and \(g(x)\le0\). Introduce slacks \(s>0\) through \(g(x)+s=0\), multipliers \(\mu>0\), and \(S=\operatorname{Diag}(s)\), \(M=\operatorname{Diag}(\mu)\). For a barrier parameter \(\tau>0\), the perturbed primal-dual KKT system is \[\nabla f(x)+J_c(x)^\top\lambda+J_g(x)^\top\mu=0,\qquad c(x)=0,\qquad g(x)+s=0,\qquad S\mu=\tau\mathbf1.\] Its Newton direction is obtained by linearizing these four residual equations jointly while maintaining step lengths for which \(s+\alpha\Delta s>0\) and \(\mu+\alpha\Delta\mu>0\). As \(\tau\downarrow0\), the last equation approaches exact complementarity.
assumptions_latex: The Jacobian of the perturbed residual system is nonsingular at the iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed equations define the perturbed primal-dual KKT representation at parameter \(\tau\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-barrier perturbation of inequality KKT complementarity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Perturbed primal-dual KKT system for nonlinear programming
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} f(x)\) subject to \(c_E(x)=0\) and \(c_I(x)\ge0\), where the functions are continuously differentiable. Introduce slacks \(s\in\mathbb{R}^q\), equality multipliers \(y\in\mathbb{R}^p\), inequality multipliers \(z\in\mathbb{R}^q\), and \(S=\operatorname{diag}(s)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth nonlinear programming with componentwise inequality slacks and a scalar positive complementarity parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\nabla f(x)-A_E(x)^Ty-A_I(x)^Tz=0,\qquad c_E(x)=0,\qquad c_I(x)-s=0,\qquad Sz=\mu e,\qquad s>0,\ z>0,\ \mu>0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The perturbed primal-dual KKT system consists of stationarity, equality feasibility, the slack equation, and the positive perturbed complementarity equations \(s_i z_i=\mu\) for every inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(x,s,y,z)\in\mathcal K_\mu\iff \begin{bmatrix}\nabla f(x)-A_E(x)^Ty-A_I(x)^Tz\\c_E(x)\\c_I(x)-s\\Sz-\mu e\end{bmatrix}=0,\quad s,z>0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The complementarity block is equivalently \(s_i z_i=\mu\) for all \(i=1,\ldots,q\).
Eliminating the positive multipliers by \(z=\mu S^{-1}e\) yields the stationarity conditions of the logarithmic-barrier problem together with primal feasibility.
special_cases_latex: At \(\mu=0\), replacing strict positivity by \(s,z\ge0\) gives the ordinary primal-dual KKT complementarity system.
When there are no equality constraints, the blocks involving \(c_E\) and \(y\) disappear.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every component satisfies \(s_i>0\) and \(z_i>0\), so no inequality is exactly complementary while \(\mu>0\).
The aggregate complementarity is \(s^Tz=q\mu\).
boundary_notes: This definition uses inequalities in the form \(c_I(x)\ge0\); reversing the convention changes multiplier signs.
A vector-valued centering target replaces \(\mu e\) in some predictor-corrector variants, but that is not the scalar central-path system defined here.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal-Dual Newton System and Fraction-to-the-Boundary Step
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Newton representation and associated positivity-preserving iteration for a smooth nonlinear program with equality and inequality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \mathcal L(x,s,y,z)=f(x)-y^Tc_{\mathrm E}(x)-z^T(c_{\mathrm I}(x)-s), S=\operatorname{diag}(s), and Z=\operatorname{diag}(z). A primal-dual Newton direction satisfies
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
\nabla_{xx}^2\mathcal L&0&-A_{\mathrm E}(x)^T&-A_{\mathrm I}(x)^T\\
0&Z&0&S\\
A_{\mathrm E}(x)&0&0&0\\
A_{\mathrm I}(x)&-I&0&0
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}p_x\\p_s\\p_y\\p_z\end{bmatrix}
=-\begin{bmatrix}
\nabla f(x)-A_{\mathrm E}(x)^Ty-A_{\mathrm I}(x)^Tz\\
Sz-\mu e\\c_{\mathrm E}(x)\\c_{\mathrm I}(x)-s
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
For \tau\in(0,1), define
\[
\alpha_s^{\max}=\max\{\alpha\in(0,1]:s+\alpha p_s\ge(1-\tau)s\},\qquad
\alpha_z^{\max}=\max\{\alpha\in(0,1]:z+\alpha p_z\ge(1-\tau)z\}.
\]
The update is
\[
(x^+,s^+)=(x,s)+\alpha_s^{\max}(p_x,p_s),\qquad
(y^+,z^+)=(y,z)+\alpha_z^{\max}(p_y,p_z),
\]
which limits how rapidly positive slacks and inequality multipliers approach zero. A residual measure is
\[
E(x,s,y,z;\mu)=\max\{\|\nabla f-A_{\mathrm E}^Ty-A_{\mathrm I}^Tz\|,\|Sz-\mu e\|,\|c_{\mathrm E}(x)\|,\|c_{\mathrm I}(x)-s\|\}.
\]
The barrier parameter may be held fixed until this perturbed KKT residual is sufficiently small or updated dynamically at every iteration. If the iterates converge to a solution satisfying second-order sufficient conditions and strict complementarity, the primal-dual matrix remains nonsingular near the solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Form the Newton system for stationarity, perturbed complementarity, equality feasibility, and the slack equations. Update the primal variables and slacks with the largest fraction-to-the-boundary step for the slacks, and update both multiplier blocks with the corresponding step for the inequality multipliers. The rule prevents positive slacks and inequality multipliers from approaching zero too rapidly. The barrier parameter can be reduced only after approximately solving each perturbed KKT system or can be updated every iteration. Near a solution satisfying second-order sufficiency and strict complementarity, the primal-dual matrix remains nonsingular.
assumptions_latex: x^*\text{ satisfies second-order sufficient conditions and strict complementarity for the local nonsingularity conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The displayed primal-dual Newton and fraction-to-the-boundary iteration preserves controlled interiority; under SOSC and strict complementarity, its coefficient matrix is locally nonsingular.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical Newton-step family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(R:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable and let \(x_k\) be a current iterate. A Newton-type realization supplies a nonsingular matrix \(B_k\) representing or modifying \(DR(x_k)\), a step length \(\alpha_k\in(0,1]\), and a step \(p_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth square systems, including stationarity equations obtained from smooth optimization; linear systems are solved accurately in this definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[B_kp_k=-R(x_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A classical Newton step solves a linearized or Newton-modified system \(B_kp_k=-R(x_k)\) and updates the iterate by \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\). The choices of \(B_k\) and \(\alpha_k\) distinguish exact, damped, derivative-approximation, and matrix-modified members of the family.
assumptions_latex: \(B_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is nonsingular and the displayed linear equation is solved without a prescribed inexact residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[p_k=-B_k^{-1}R(x_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kB_k^{-1}R(x_k).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The step is the zero of the affine model \(M_k(x_k+p)=R(x_k)+B_kp\).
special_cases_latex: Exact Newton uses \(B_k=DR(x_k)\) and \(\alpha_k=1\).
Damped Newton uses \(B_k=DR(x_k)\) and \(0<\alpha_k<1\).
For unconstrained minimization, \(R=\nabla f\) and the exact coefficient matrix is \(DR=\nabla^2f\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(R\) is affine and \(B_k=DR\) is nonsingular, one full exact step solves \(R(x)=0\).
The definition separates modification of the Newton equation through \(B_k\) from damping through \(\alpha_k\).
boundary_notes: Inexact Newton methods, which permit a nonzero linear-system residual, are outside this classical accurately-solved family.
Trust-region steps that do not lie on the Newton direction need a separate model-subproblem definition.
